Hybrid RAS shells were fabricated using glass fiber/epoxy/carbon-black (5 wt%) as absorbing layers and carbon fiber reinforced epoxy as reflection layers.
The shells were shaped into three-dimensional 'C' and 'U' geometries.
Carbon-black nanoparticles used had an average diameter of about 40 nm and high surface area (950 cm2/g).
Curing was performed at 120°C and 5.5 atm in an autoclave for 2 hours.
Spring-back deformation was compensated by designing aluminum molds with additional bending angles.
Finite element analysis (ANSYS 8.0) predicted spring-back behavior with about 21.8% average error compared to experiments.
The radar cross section (RCS) was measured at 10 GHz using a compact range method.
Hybrid RAS shells achieved an average radar absorption efficiency of about 11 dB compared to perfect electric conductor shells.
Reflection coefficient of CFRP was about 120 dB, considered as a perfect electric conductor (PEC) in this study.
The physical optics method was used to predict RCS, showing good agreement with experimental results (errors under 7%).
The spring-back angle for zero deformation was approximately -4.29° for 'C' shape and -1.9° for 'U' shape molds.
Mechanical properties used in FEA: Elastic modulus of 20.8 GPa for GFRP-CB and 81.2 GPa for CFRP.
Thermal expansion coefficients were measured and applied in the FEA to simulate curing effects.
The hybrid structure offers a higher stiffness-to-weight ratio compared to metallic reflection layers.
The study confirms that controlling mold bending angles can effectively eliminate spring-back in hybrid composite shells.
Radar absorption efficiency was highest (~15 dB) in certain rotational angles for the 'C' shape shell.
The study used a three-phase composite prepreg with nano carbon-black mixed into epoxy resin.
The hybrid RAS shells protect electromagnetic wave transmission to the reflection layer while maintaining structural strength.
The research was supported by the Agency for Defense Development and Brain Korea 21 projects.
Further investigations are required for applying hybrid RAS to complex military structures and severe environments.
